channel.title: Astronomy (2026) — Research Digest
channel.description: Recent curated links for Astronomy in 2026, including short summaries and source URLs.

item.title: Astronomers watch 1st black hole ever imaged launch a 3,000-light-year-long cosmic jet from its glowing 'shadow'
item.description: Using Event Horizon Telescope data combined with VLBI, researchers linked the base of M87*’s powerful jet to the glowing ring of material around the black hole, revealing radio emission from within a tenth of a light-year of the event horizon and offering new constraints on how supermassive black holes launch jets. The results appear in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

item.title: February's night sky brings a planetary parade, Orion and the Artemis II launch
item.description: A skywatching guide highlights February’s line-up of planets—Venus, Mercury, Saturn, and Jupiter—best viewing windows just after sunset, tips for observing Orion and Betelgeuse, and context about NASA’s upcoming Artemis II lunar mission.

item.title: U.S. Naval Observatory adopts FSU binary star research
item.description: Ferris State University researchers produced updated orbital models for six visual binary star systems; four were incorporated in January 2026 into the Sixth Catalog of Orbits of Visual Binary Stars, improving datasets that astronomers use to study stellar motion and mass.

item.title: Supernova Remnant Cassiopeia A
item.description: An Astronomy Picture of the Day feature explains the life cycle of massive stars using Cassiopeia A as an example, describing how heavy elements forged in stellar cores are dispersed by supernovae into interstellar space, with an accompanying high-resolution image of the remnant.

item.title: News in Astronomy & Geophysics – February 2026
item.description: A monthly roundup of notable developments across astronomy and geophysics, highlighting recent research results, mission updates, and community news. Provides concise context and links for further reading.

item.title: See February's full Snow Moon rise this weekend next to a glittering star cluster
item.description: Guide to viewing the February 1 Snow Moon as it appears near the Beehive Cluster (M44), with best times and simple observing tips. Explains where to look and how binoculars enhance the star cluster’s view.

item.title: The Snow Moon will 'swallow' one of the brightest stars in the sky this weekend: Where and when to look
item.description: Explains a lunar occultation of Regulus on February 2, including visibility regions and city-by-city timing. Offers practical advice for watching the star disappear and reappear behind the Moon.

item.title: February 2026: What's in the sky this month? Jupiter continues to dominate the night; Mercury, Venus, and Saturn are visible
item.description: Monthly skywatching forecast covering planetary visibility and noteworthy conjunctions. Highlights Jupiter’s prominence, Mercury and Venus in the west after sunset, and Neptune’s close pairing with Saturn.

item.title: NASA reveals a rare six-planet parade across February's evening sky
item.description: Reports on a monthlong alignment of six planets visible after sunset throughout February, with best viewing in late month. Describes where to look and why the event unfolds over multiple evenings rather than peaking on one night.

item.title: Milky Way shines over Gemini South Observatory | Space photo of the day for Jan. 26, 2025
item.description: A striking astrophotograph shows the Milky Way arcing over Gemini South on Cerro Pachón, highlighting the International Gemini Observatory’s role in optical/IR astronomy, use of adaptive optics, and push toward sustainable operations with on-site solar power.

item.title: Super-Earth exoplanets may have built-in magnetic protection from churning magma - and that's good news for life
item.description: Reporting on new Nature Astronomy research, this article describes how super-Earths could sustain magnetic fields driven by iron-rich basal magma oceans deep within their interiors, potentially shielding atmospheres and boosting habitability prospects.

item.title: Furthest galaxy EVER spotted is seen in 'time travel' image from just 280 million years after Big Bang, Nasa reveals
item.description: The piece covers JWST observations of galaxy MoM-z14 at redshift ∼14.4, seen 280 million years after the Big Bang, noting unusual nitrogen enrichment that hints at massive early stars and challenges assumptions about early galaxy evolution.

item.title: Rethinking the cosmos: UGA astronomy research shakes up the heavens
item.description: UGA’s Cassandra Hall is profiled for work on planet formation and the proposed “photosynthetic habitable zone,” with observational support from systems like AB Aurigae illustrating how disks can validate theoretical predictions.

item.title: NGC 1333: Stellar Nursery in Perseus
item.description: A telescopic close-up of reflection nebula NGC 1333, about 1,000 light-years away in Perseus, reveals dusty filaments, newborn star clusters, and red emission from Herbig–Haro jets and shocked gas—evidence of active, recent star formation in this nearby molecular cloud.

item.title: LDN 1622: Dark Nebula in Orion
item.description: A deep image highlights the Boogeyman Nebula (LDN 1622) silhouetted against faint hydrogen glow near Barnard’s Loop in Orion, revealing hidden young stars and a nearby reflection nebula (vdB 62) about 1,500 light-years away.

item.title: Planetary Nebula Abell 7
item.description: Long exposures with narrowband filters uncover the faint, 8-light-year-wide shell of Abell 7 in Lepus—an aging, sun-like star’s ejected layers—set about 1,800 light-years away and textured by intricate hydrogen and oxygen emission.

item.title: Earthset from Orion
item.description: A camera on NASA’s Artemis I Orion spacecraft captured Earth setting behind the Moon on Nov. 21, 2022, during a close lunar flyby that helped insert Orion into a distant retrograde orbit for the uncrewed test mission.

item.title: Phobos: Doomed Moon of Mars
item.description: HiRISE imagery shows cratered Phobos, which orbits Mars so closely that tidal forces are slowly pulling it inward; models suggest it will break apart into a debris ring in roughly 50 million years.

item.title: Active Galactic Nuclei SIG Inaugural Spotlight Series on Tuesday, January 27, 2026
item.description: NASA’s AGN Science Interest Group launches a monthly seminar series to showcase new AGN results and foster community discussion, with the kickoff featuring talks on multiphase AGN feedback and JWST-based insights into local AGN.

item.title: Severe G4 geomagnetic storm sparks jaw-dropping northern lights worldwide (photos)
item.description: A fast coronal mass ejection from a powerful X1.9 solar flare triggered a severe G4 geomagnetic storm, producing vivid auroras far into mid-latitudes across Europe, North America and Asia. The piece compiles striking images, explains the storm’s rapid onset, and notes the potential for additional auroral activity as space weather remains unsettled.

item.title: See a slender crescent moon shine with Saturn in the western sky tonight
item.description: On the evening of Jan. 22, a 22%-lit crescent moon appears near Saturn in the southwest, separated by about 7 degrees. The article offers observing tips, noting Saturn’s rings are nearly edge-on and that larger backyard telescopes can reveal moons like Titan and Rhea; Neptune lies nearby but requires more aperture.

item.title: New moon of January 2026 brings prime views of Jupiter, Saturn and winter stars tonight
item.description: With the new moon providing dark skies, observers get prime views of Jupiter in Gemini, Saturn in the early evening, and bright winter constellations including Orion and Canis Major. The guide highlights how to locate key stars such as Sirius, Betelgeuse and Rigel, and offers practical sky-hopping advice.

item.title: Comet Wierzchos buzzes the sun later today: But can you see it?
item.description: Comet C/2024 E1 (Wierzchos) reached perihelion on January 20, 2026, brightening to about magnitude +8.1. It isn’t naked‑eye visible but can be seen with small telescopes; first best from the Southern Hemisphere, then reappearing for Northern observers in mid‑February as it recedes from the Sun.

item.title: Barred Spiral Galaxy NGC 1365 from Webb
item.description: A JWST MIRI image reveals intricate dust lanes, star‑forming regions, and the strong bar of NGC 1365—an immense barred spiral about 200,000 light‑years across and ~56 million light‑years away—captured in mid‑infrared detail.

item.title: 'Best show in 20 years' - Beautiful timelapse of Northern Lights captured in Donegal after aurora borealis above Ireland
item.description: A strong geomagnetic storm on January 20 lit up skies across Ireland; a Donegal timelapse shows vivid pink and green auroras, with unusually widespread visibility attributed to intense solar activity.

item.title: Chinese New Year 2026: Witness the rare 'ring of fire' solar eclipse and 'fire horse year' celebrations across the globe
item.description: Chinese New Year in 2026 will coincide with a rare annular (‘ring of fire’) solar eclipse, creating a notable overlap of cultural celebrations with a major astronomical event.

item.title: Massive black hole mystery unlocked by researchers
item.description: A report highlights new research from Maynooth University proposing how supermassive black holes could have grown so rapidly in the early universe, offering a potential solution to their unexpectedly large masses.

item.title: NGC 55: A Galaxy of Nebulas
item.description: A 50-hour narrowband exposure isolates hydrogen (Hα) and oxygen ([O III]) emission to reveal widespread nebulae threaded across the nearly edge-on galaxy NGC 55, showing how targeted filters expose faint structures otherwise missed in broadband images.

item.title: CTB 1: The Medulla Nebula
item.description: The supernova remnant CTB 1 in Cassiopeia—likely from a massive star that exploded ~10,000 years ago—shows a brain-like shell glowing in visible light from shock-heated gas; puzzling X-ray emission highlights ongoing research into its energetic processes.

item.title: NGC 55: A Galaxy of Nebulas
item.description: A deep, narrowband view of edge-on galaxy NGC 55 isolates hydrogen and oxygen emission to reveal widespread nebulae and star-forming complexes across the disk, demonstrating how targeted filters can uncover faint structures in external galaxies.

item.title: Revolutionary imaging of black hole aims to prove they are not 'evil vacuum cleaners'
item.description: Event Horizon Telescope astronomers are preparing a campaign to create the first time-lapse 'movie' of a supermassive black hole (M87*), stitching frequent observations from a global radio array to probe spin and jet formation and better understand black hole growth.

item.title: Astronomers confirm earliest Milky Way-like galaxy in the universe, just 2 billion years after the Big Bang
item.description: Using JWST imaging and Keck/MOSFIRE spectroscopy, researchers confirmed COSMOS-74706 as the most distant barred spiral known, showing complex Milky Way–like structure existed over 11.5 billion years ago and tightening timelines for galaxy evolution.

item.title: Scots can sleep under stars during rare & spectacular planetary event for FREE - find out how
item.description: A six-planet alignment expected in late February 2026 is spurring a stargazing promotion at Galloway Forest Park, highlighting dark-sky tourism and offering public observing with astronomy gear during the celestial lineup.

item.title: How to find 4 legendary spacecraft in January's night sky
item.description: This guide helps skywatchers locate the regions of the sky where JWST, Europa Clipper, JUICE, and Voyager 1 currently reside. It offers star-hopping tips, notes on each mission’s position relative to constellations, and practical observing advice. While the craft are not visible to the naked eye, the article points to nearby celestial landmarks worth viewing.

item.title: NASA's powerful new Roman Space Telescope is complete - and will soon begin mission to find 100,000 alien worlds
item.description: NASA has finished assembling the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, a wide-field infrared observatory designed to probe dark energy, map the Milky Way’s center, and discover tens of thousands of exoplanets. The mission is targeting an L2 orbit and could launch as early as fall 2026, with instruments including the 288-megapixel Wide Field Instrument and a cutting-edge coronagraph.

item.title: Aurora australis set to light up Australian sky as agencies monitor 'severe' solar storm
item.description: A strong solar storm triggered by a January 18 flare is enhancing auroral activity, with potential sightings as far north as southern Australia and parts of New Zealand. Agencies are monitoring possible impacts on satellites, GPS, and power systems, though experts say immediate risks are limited.

item.title: Integrating The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's Two Halves
item.description: NASA released a media update marking the integration of Roman’s telescope and instruments onto the instrument carrier, completing the payload. The team is now moving to join the payload to the spacecraft—an assembly milestone ahead of final testing and launch preparations.

item.title: Astronomers baffled by 'mysterious disruptor' with a mass of 1 million suns and a black hole for a heart
item.description: Report on a newly detected, completely dark object about 11 billion light-years away whose lensing ‘disruptions’ reveal a ~1-million-solar-mass body with a compact, black-hole-like core and an extended disk. Its unusual mass distribution challenges standard dark-matter expectations; follow-up (e.g., JWST) could clarify whether it’s a faint ultracompact galaxy or a novel dark object.

item.title: Astronomers searching for alien life are sharpening our cosmic clocks. Here's why
item.description: News feature on recent work refining pulsar timing by measuring how interstellar electrons subtly delay radio pulses (nanosecond-level effects) from PSR J0332+5434 using the Allen Telescope Array. The improved modeling boosts precision for gravitational-wave searches and helps discriminate genuine technosignatures from noise in SETI observations.

item.title: Rare Near-Opposition Alignment of 3I/ATLAS on 22 January, 2026
item.description: Paper highlighting that the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS will align within ~0.69° of the Earth–Sun axis on 2026-01-22, enabling unique measurements of opposition surge and polarimetric properties of interstellar dust. The authors outline observing geometry and requirements to constrain albedo, structure, and composition.

item.title: 6AC4721
item.description: Entry describing a newly discovered Kreutz sungrazer comet (found 2026-01-13 by the MAPS program). It was unusually distant at discovery, ~17.8 mag, and follows a highly inclined (~144.5°) orbit. The comet’s perihelion is expected in early April 2026 with an estimated orbital period of ~852 years.

item.title: BlackCAT
item.description: Overview of NASA’s BlackCAT (Black Hole Coded Aperture Telescope), a 6U CubeSat X‑ray astronomy mission built by Penn State. Launched on 2026-01-11 to a dawn/dusk sun‑synchronous orbit, it will monitor gamma‑ray bursts and other high‑energy transients for ~14 months to support time‑domain and multi‑messenger astronomy.

item.title: Astronomy and Astrophysics Advisory Committee meeting on 29-30 January 2026
item.description: Announcement of a hybrid AAAC meeting to advise NSF, NASA, and DOE on astronomy and astrophysics priorities, covering policy and programmatic issues across the field.

item.title: Discovery of a Starless Galaxy Reported at AAS
item.description: Brief news item noting the report of a starless galaxy at the AAS meeting, highlighting its implications for galaxy formation and dark matter studies.

item.title: M104: The Sombrero Galaxy in Infrared
item.description: APOD explains a composite view of the Sombrero Galaxy combining Spitzer infrared and Hubble visible light, revealing the dust lane’s bright IR glow and the galaxy’s structure.

item.title: A Solar Eruption from SDO
item.description: Astronomy Picture of the Day highlights a towering solar plasma eruption captured by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory, marking the onset of a coronal mass ejection. The explanation notes the immense scale of the structure and how SDO’s continuous monitoring improves space‑weather forecasting and understanding of solar impacts on technology.

item.title: Plato and the Lunar Alps
item.description: APOD features a high‑resolution telescopic view of the Moon’s crater Plato and the Montes Alpes. The note explains that the lunar Alps formed from the Mare Imbrium impact, contrasts this with tectonic uplift on Earth’s Alps, and points out the straight Alpine Valley (Vallis Alpes) cutting through the range.

item.title: Jupiter will outshine every star in the sky this weekend - how to see the 'king of planets' at opposition
item.description: Jupiter reaches opposition on January 10, 2026, shining brighter than any star and remaining visible all night. The guide explains when and where to look, and what you can see with binoculars or a small telescope, including the Galilean moons and cloud bands. It also notes other upcoming sky events featuring Jupiter.

item.title: Jupiter with the Great Red Spot
item.description: Published the day Jupiter reached opposition, this APOD features a high-resolution image showing the planet’s cloud belts and the Great Red Spot. The accompanying explanation discusses why opposition brings peak brightness and viewing conditions. The image, captured days earlier, showcases fine atmospheric detail.

item.title: AAS Names Recipients of 2026 Awards & Prizes
item.description: The American Astronomical Society announced its 2026 research and education prize recipients, including top honors such as the Henry Norris Russell Lectureship, recognizing major contributions across astronomy.

item.title: AAS Names 23 New Fellows for 2026
item.description: The AAS honored 23 members as 2026 Fellows for achievements in research, instrumentation, education, outreach, and service to the astronomical community.

item.title: Highlights from AAS Nova: 14 December 2025 – 10 January 2026
item.description: A roundup of recent AAS journal research and AAS 247 meeting coverage, touching on early spiral structure in galaxies, pulsar-timing gravitational-wave astronomy, baryon acoustic oscillation measurements, brown dwarfs, and starburst galaxies.

item.title: Vera C. Rubin Observatory discovers enormous, record-breaking asteroid in first 7 nights of observations
item.description: In its first week of early observations, Rubin found asteroid 2025 MN45 (~710 m wide) spinning once every ~113 seconds—the fastest-known rotation for an asteroid over 500 m. The result, part of the first LSST Camera–based paper, implies a strong, likely monolithic body and previews the survey’s potential after revealing ~1,900 new asteroids.

item.title: Empirical Evidence of Planetary Group Configurations Modulating Solar Activity
item.description: Analyzing daily sunspot counts from 1935–2024, the authors find that specific 90° planetary group configurations coincide with reduced sunspot variability and a typical decline in activity ~21 days post-event. They argue these patterns support a planetary influence on solar activity and point to testable events later in 2026.

item.title: Simeis 147: The Spaghetti Nebula Supernova Remnant
item.description: APOD highlights the sprawling supernova remnant Simeis 147 (Sharpless 2-240), a web of filaments near the Taurus–Auriga border spanning ~3° on the sky—about 150 light-years across at an estimated distance of ~3,000 light-years—captured in a richly detailed mosaic.

item.title: Lightcurves, Rotation Periods, and Colors for Vera C. Rubin Observatory's First Asteroid Discoveries
item.description: Commissioning-time observations from the Rubin Observatory report lightcurves and colors for its first asteroid finds, revealing several super- to ultra-fast rotators hundreds of meters across. The results push known rotation-rate limits for sub‑kilometer main-belt asteroids and suggest implications for their internal strength and collisional histories.

item.title: Vera C. Rubin Observatory spots record-breaking asteroid in pre-survey observations
item.description: A Rubin Observatory team reports record-fast-spinning, sub‑kilometer main-belt asteroids detected during early commissioning. The discovery, summarized here with links to the ApJL paper, highlights how Rubin’s cadence can expose extreme rotators and improve understanding of asteroid composition and cohesion prior to the full LSST survey.

item.title: Jupiter is at its best and brightest of 2026 tonight! Here's what to expect as the gas giant reaches opposition
item.description: Jupiter reaches opposition on January 9–10, 2026, shining around magnitude −2.7 in Gemini and spanning roughly 45.6 arcseconds. The guide explains when and where to look, what telescopes can reveal in the cloud bands, and how to catch the changing configurations of the four Galilean moons throughout the night.

item.title: Comet 24P/Schaumasse makes its closest approach to the sun today: But will you be able to see it?
item.description: At perihelion on January 8, 2026, periodic comet 24P/Schaumasse brightened but remained near magnitude +10.8—too faint for naked‑eye viewing. The piece details where to find it near Virgo’s star Vindemiatrix, the best predawn observing windows, and why moonlight and the comet’s faintness make telescopic aid essential.

item.title: January belongs to Jupiter: See the king of planets in the night sky this month
item.description: A monthlong observing guide to Jupiter at its 2026 peak: the article covers its January 10 opposition, visibility in Gemini, closest approach around January 9, and tips for spotting atmospheric details and the Galilean moons, along with notable alignments and observing opportunities through the month.

item.title: Meteor Dust
item.description: Astronomy Picture of the Day explains how a bright meteor sheds heated material as it streaks through Earth’s atmosphere, creating a brief dust trail that winds disperse within minutes. The featured Geminids image, captured by Xu Chen, illustrates this process and notes that much of the dust ultimately settles to Earth.

item.title: Jupiter's Clouds in High Definition from Juno
item.description: Using data from NASA’s Juno mission, APOD features a high-definition view of Jupiter’s cloud tops and summarizes key findings: a complex, multipolar magnetic field and atmospheric structure extending hundreds of kilometers below the visible cloud deck. The processed imagery showcases turbulent bands and vortices.

item.title: What’s Up: January 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA
item.description: NASA’s monthly guide spotlights January highlights for observers, including Jupiter at opposition on Jan. 10, a Moon–Saturn conjunction on Jan. 23, and advice for spotting the Beehive Cluster (M44). It offers practical tips for when and where to look and suggests binoculars or small telescopes for best views.

item.title: Cosmic Origins at AAS 247
item.description: An overview of NASA’s Cosmic Origins presence at the American Astronomical Society’s 247th meeting (Jan. 4–8, Phoenix), listing sessions on AGN, AI/ML, infrared science, and joint PAG updates. It also points to NASA press releases and program updates shared during the conference week.

item.title: Earliest, hottest galaxy cluster gas on record challenges cosmological models
item.description: An international team reports Sunyaev–Zel’dovich detection of extremely hot intracluster gas just 1.4 billion years after the Big Bang (z≈4.3). The result implies earlier and more intense heating—likely tied to active black holes—than standard cluster formation models predict, prompting a reassessment of how quickly clusters assemble.

item.title: The 2026 'Super Bowl of Astronomy' starts today - here's what's happening
item.description: Preview of the American Astronomical Society’s 247th meeting (Jan. 4–8, Phoenix) highlighting new results on exoplanets, galaxy evolution and cosmic origins, with sessions on NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory and the upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, plus online press briefings and community programming.

item.title: Carina Nebula shines with white-blue stars photo of the day for Jan. 5, 2026 | Space
item.description: A JWST image of the Westerlund 2 cluster in the Carina Nebula reveals a rich population of low-mass objects including brown dwarfs down to ~10 Jupiter masses, helping test how intense radiation fields affect the initial mass function in extreme star-forming regions.

item.title: Hunting for the First Explosions at the High-Redshift Frontier
item.description: Using cosmological simulations, the authors show that pair‑instability supernovae from Population III stars could occur at z≈30–40 and be detectable by JWST, potentially explaining some extreme high‑redshift candidates and offering a way to probe the epoch of first star formation.

item.title: What looked like a planet was actually a massive space collision
item.description: Hubble observations of the nearby star Fomalhaut revealed bright debris clouds from colossal collisions between large space rocks. One cloud was previously mistaken for an exoplanet before fading; seeing two such events in two decades suggests giant impacts may be more common in young systems than thought.

item.title: A planet just vanished. NASA’s Hubble reveals a violent cosmic secret
item.description: Astronomers studying a nearby star system found that a supposed exoplanet abruptly disappeared, and another bright object appeared nearby. Reanalysis of years of Hubble data indicates the signals were actually dust clouds from massive collisions between asteroid-sized bodies, not planets.

item.title: The largest sun of 2026 rises today as Earth draws closest to our parent star
item.description: Explains Earth’s Jan. 3 perihelion—when our planet is closest to the Sun—why the Sun appears slightly larger then, and why seasons are set by axial tilt rather than distance.

item.title: January 2026: What's in the sky this month?
item.description: A monthly observing guide covering planetary visibility and notable events like transits of Jupiter’s moons, with dates and times to help backyard observers plan sessions.

item.title: The 1st full moon of 2026 rises tonight! Here's what to expect from January's supermoon Wolf Moon
item.description: January’s Wolf Moon was also a supermoon, appearing brighter and slightly larger as it coincided with the moon’s close approach to Earth. The article offers viewing tips, notes the time of peak brightness, and highlights nearby sights like Jupiter for observers and astrophotographers.

item.title: One of the best meteor showers of the year peaks at the worst possible time this week
item.description: The Quadrantid meteor shower peaked on January 3, 2026, but poor timing for North America and a bright full moon significantly reduced visibility. The piece explains the shower’s brief, intense peak and its likely association with asteroid 2003 EH1.

item.title: SpaceX launches Italian Earth-observing satellite to orbit on the 1st mission of 2026 (video)
item.description: On January 2, 2026, SpaceX launched a COSMO-SkyMed Second Generation radar satellite for the Italian Space Agency and Ministry of Defence, marking the year’s first orbital mission. The Falcon 9 first stage landed successfully after its 21st flight, underscoring the company’s rapid reusability cadence.

item.title: Auroral Corona
item.description: A panoramic mosaic captures a striking auroral corona above Kirkjufell, Iceland, with the explanation noting how Solar Cycle 25’s strong activity fueled frequent 2025 auroras and is expected to continue into 2026.

item.title: Full Moonlight
item.description: A photo essay on the first Full Moon of 2026, occurring hours before Earth’s perihelion; it highlights the Moon’s recent perigee and Jupiter appearing nearby in the night sky.

item.title: Jupiter's Clouds in High Definition from Juno
item.description: Imagery from NASA’s Juno mission illustrates Jupiter’s complex atmospheric structures and non‑dipolar magnetic field, with radio data indicating organization extending hundreds of kilometers below the cloud tops.

item.title: STARS Over Springfield
item.description: Event listing detailing a public astronomy program with a lecture, planetarium show, and views through the 20‑inch Fillmore telescope at the Springfield Science Museum.

item.title: Public Observing Event - George Observatory
item.description: Public stargazing session hosted by Fort Bend Astronomy Club at the George Observatory, offering guided views of visible evening objects away from city lights.

item.title: Auroral Corona
item.description: A striking auroral corona over Kirkjufell, Iceland captured during a strong geomagnetic storm illustrates how the ongoing Solar Cycle 25 maximum is boosting aurora activity. The display, shown in a 21‑frame panoramic mosaic, reveals energetic curtains of light converging overhead.

item.title: The Red Rectangle Nebula from Hubble
item.description: Hubble imagery of the Red Rectangle highlights its unusual X‑shaped appearance, likely sculpted by a thick dust torus around an aging binary star system. The configuration pinches a more spherical outflow into opposing cones that produce the nebula’s distinctive geometry and colors.

item.title: COPAG Activities at AAS 247
item.description: NASA’s Cosmic Origins Program announces COPAG and Joint‑PAG sessions at the American Astronomical Society’s 247th meeting in Phoenix on January 4, 2026. The events include community discussions and a Q&A with NASA Astrophysics Division Director Shawn Domagal‑Goldman.

item.title: 15 skywatching events you won't want to miss in 2026
item.description: A year-ahead guide highlights 2026’s top celestial events, including a total lunar eclipse on Mar. 2–3 and a rare total solar eclipse on Aug. 12. It also lists key planetary conjunctions, major meteor showers, and a bright Christmas Eve supermoon.

item.title: Earth at Perihelion: What happens when we're nearest to the sun
item.description: Explains Earth’s perihelion on Jan 3, 2026 (12:15 p.m. EST/17:15 UTC): seasons are set by axial tilt, not distance; Earth moves slightly faster in its orbit at perihelion. ([timesofindia.indiatimes.com](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/etimes/trending/earth-at-perihelion-what-happens-when-were-nearest-to-the-sun/articleshow/126284845.cms?utm_source=openai))
